 Florida dengue outbreak raises travel insurance concerns for winter visitors 
 Travel Risk Management 
 17 Nov 2026
 | 
 Siân Yates 
 Share 
 A record rise in locally transmitted infections around Tampa Bay highlights medical assistance and coverage considerations for international travellers
 Florida has recorded 624 locally acquired cases of dengue fever in 2026, its largest outbreak in decades, raising concerns over medical expenses and insurance coverage for international visitors.
 Figures published by the Florida Department of Health on 13 November, covering the week ending 7 November, show that Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa, has recorded 468 cases, while neighbouring Pinellas County has reported 109. The latest report recorded 100 additional locally acquired cases, bringing the statewide total to more than three times the 199 cases reported in 2023.
 The outbreak coincides with the arrival of Canadian snowbirds , many of whom spend extended periods in Florida during the winter months.
 Global Affairs Canada issued a dengue outbreak monitoring alert in October, although its overall travel advice for the US remains unchanged.
 Dengue is transmitted through infected mosquito bites and can cause fever, severe headaches, and muscle and joint pain. While most infections are mild or asymptomatic, severe cases can require hospitalisation.
 For international visitors, treatment in the US can result in substantial medical expenses, particularly as Canadian provincial healthcare plans provide limited reimbursement for care received abroad.
 Travel medical insurance may cover emergency treatment for dengue, although claims remain subject to policy conditions, including pre-existing medical conditions, trip duration limits, and applicable travel advisories. These considerations are particularly relevant for older travellers and those spending several months overseas, whose policies may include medical stability requirements or restrictions on the length of their stay.
 Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency until 19 November as authorities continue mosquito control operations to limit the spread of the virus.
 Health officials are advising residents and visitors to use insect repellent, wear protective clothing, and eliminate standing water where mosquitoes can breed.
